body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The nanobind wrappers (`RDK_BUILD_NANOBIND_WRAPPERS`) are intended to be a drop-in replacement for the Boost.Python wrappers, but they differ from them, and from what their own signatures promise: many parameters are typed as a bare `object`, some functions hang or raise on input the Boost wrappers accept, and a few exceptions and argument names differ. This issue tracks the pull requests that address them.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

What an argument accepts follows from what it is:

| argument | C++ type | accepts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| filesystem path | `std::filesystem::path` | `str`, `bytes`, `os.PathLike` |
| serialized input — SMILES, SMARTS, Mol/PDB/CDXML blocks | `StringOrBytes` | `str`, `bytes` |
| identifier — property keys, property-query names, tags, delimiters, option strings | `std::string` | `str` |


Pull requests:

- [ ] #9591 — Type parameters and return values instead of `nb::object`, following the rule above and how each value is used, with wrong types raising `TypeError` at the call boundary. Also matches the Boost wrappers on argument names, `ValueError`/`IndexError`, filenames and the inputs several functions accept. (Inspired by a question from Andrew Dalke at the RDKit UGM.)
- [ ] #9613 — Commit stubs generated by `nanobind.stubgen` and install them beside the modules with `rdkit/py.typed`, so type checkers read the signatures #9591 writes. Committing them is what gets stubs into conda-forge's cross-compiled packages, whose builds cannot import the modules to generate them. Builds on #9591.
- [ ] #9597 — ChemDraw fixes in both wrapper sets: `rdChemDraw` imports `rdChemReactions`, the readers detect CDX instead of assuming CDXML and take an explicit `format` (#9604), and `testChemDraw.py` runs.

Related fixes found along the way:

- [ ] #9612 — Add the missing `<vector>` include to `RealValueVect.h`, remove the duplicated test methods in `testGeometry.py`, and make the root `CONTRIBUTING` pointer a real link.
- [ ] #9615 — Boost wrapper fixes with no nanobind counterpart: `GetMorganFeatureAtomInvGen` extracted its `patterns` as a `std::vector<const ROMol *>`, which no converter produces from a list or a tuple, so it used the default feature definitions, and fixing it changes the fingerprints callers get when they pass `patterns`; and a stream built on an object with no `read` yielded nothing instead of raising.
- [ ] #9611 — Fix crashes on generators, suppliers and lazy sequences, where wrappers kept raw pointers to freed elements, in nanobind and in several Boost wrappers. Also rejects a `None` reagent in `EnumerateLibrary`, fixes `list()` on a fresh `SmilesMolSupplier`, and checks that FreeSASA `radii` has one entry per atom.

Remaining work, not yet in a pull request:

- [ ] Type the `nb::object` parameters #9591 leaves, whose type does not follow from how they are used:
  - arguments written back into by index or `append`: `FragmentOnBonds`' `cutsPerAtom`, the layered and pattern fingerprints' `atomCounts`, `AlignMolConformers`' `RMSlist`, `ConvertToNumpyArray`'s `destArray`
  - arguments that take more than one kind of value: `ReplaceCore`'s `match` and the `matches` arguments, the shape options' `customFeatures`, `TautomerEnumerator.SetCallback` (a callable or a `TautomerEnumeratorCallback`), `PickCanonical`'s `iterable` (an enumeration result or molecules), the `rdFMCS` comparators (an enum or an `MCSAtomCompare`/`MCSBondCompare` subclass), `GetTanimotoDistMat`/`GetTanimotoSimMat`' `bitVectList` and the `InfoTheory` rankers' `bitVect` (explicit or sparse bit vectors), `GetEuclideanDistMat`'s `descripMat` (an array or a sequence of vectors), `ChemicalReaction.ToBinary`'s `propertyFlags` (an int or a `PropertyPickleOptions`), and `rdAlignment`'s points
  - `rdMIF`'s `charges` and `positions`, which raise `ValueError` for a non-sequence, so typing them would change that to `TypeError`
  - ignored arguments: `useCache`, the reduced-graph `atomTypes`
  - Python file objects and `__exit__` arguments stay `object`
- [ ] Decide the argument names that differ between the two wrapper sets. Comparing the generated signatures of both builds found these beyond the ones #9591 names. Each breaks a keyword that works against the Boost wrappers, but each also looks deliberate:

  | function | Boost | nanobind | notes |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `Mol.GetNumAtoms`, `RWMol.GetNumAtoms`, `PropertyMol.GetNumAtoms` | `onlyHeavy` | absent | the Boost wrapper logs "the onlyHeavy argument to mol.GetNumAtoms() has been deprecated" |
  | `BondFromSmarts` | `SMILES` | `SMARTS` | nanobind is the correct one; the Boost docstring names the wrong language |
  | `MMFFGetMoleculeForceField` | `pyMMFFMolProperties` | `MMFFMolProperties` | drops a `py` prefix that describes the wrapper rather than the argument |
  | `GetO3A`, `GetO3AForProbeConfs` | `prbPyMMFFMolProperties`, `refPyMMFFMolProperties` | `prbMMFFMolProperties`, `refMMFFMolProperties` | same `py` prefix |
  | `GetMoleculeBoundsMatrix` | `embedParams` | `embedParameters` | spells the word out |
  | `Atom.Match`, `QueryAtom.Match` | `what` | `other` | `other` reads better and matches the `Point` methods |
  | `SubstructMatchParameters.setExtraAtomCheckFunc` | `atomCoordsMatcher` | `func` | describes the parameter rather than one expected argument type |
  | `FilterCatalog.AddEntry` | `updateFPLength` | absent | the argument itself is gone, not just its name |
  | `MHFPEncoder.EncodeSECFPMol`, `EncodeSECFPMolsBulk` | `smiles` | `mol`, `mols` | the argument takes a different type here, so this is more than a rename |

- [ ] Fix two crashes, in both wrapper sets: `rdMolCatalog.MolCatalogEntry().GetMol()` dereferences the entry's null molecule, and `TautomerEnumerator().PickCanonical([])` dereferences a null best molecule (`Tautomer.h`). Both segfault.
- [ ] Rewrite the nanobind docstrings in Google style (`Args:`, `Returns:`, `Raises:`), so the stubs from #9613 carry them. Pyright, which Pylance is built on, reads a function's docstring from its stub and falls back to a `.py` source only when the stub has none, so for a compiled module the stub is the only place an editor can show one; its Markdown conversion handles Google `Args:` sections, reST and Epytext fields. The docstrings use RDKit's own `ARGUMENTS:`/`RETURNS:` layout: 427 `ARGUMENTS:` sections across 30 stubs, written in 51 nanobind wrapper source files, and no `Args:` sections. The Boost wrappers keep separate copies of these docstrings, so `help()` output would differ between the wrapper sets unless both are rewritten.
- [ ] Clean up the idioms the nanobind wrappers inherited, each only where it is worth the churn. Counting on #9591's branch: 115 `attr("name")()` calls, most into Python objects the wrapper does not own and so unavoidable; 95 `nb::len()` calls, of which the ones on a typed container can be `size()`; and 26 `nb::cast<nb::dict/list/tuple>()` calls, of which the ones on a parameter mean the parameter should carry the type instead, while the rest convert an element, which is how a handle is indexed. #9591 types the three descriptor lists this way. The Boost counterpart, 40 tests that compare a `python::object` with a default-constructed one rather than asking `is_none()`, is #9619.
- [ ] Give `rdMIF` an error type of its own, if it should have one. #9591 removes `MIFValueError`/`MIFIndexError` because they were aliases for the shared `ValueErrorException`/`IndexErrorException`; a MIF-specific Python error needs a MIF-specific C++ exception class and new throw sites.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Matching the Boost wrappers exactly everywhere. That turned out not to be a consistent target: Boost accepts `bytes` wherever a parameter is declared `std::string` and rejects it wherever one is declared `const char *`, regardless of meaning — `Atom.SetProp(b'k', ...)` works while `Bond.SetProp(b'k', ...)` does not — and RDKit registers its `pathlib.Path` converter for every `std::string` parameter, not only filenames. Accepting `bytes` for identifiers also lets a non-UTF-8 key be stored, after which `GetPropNames()` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, so identifiers stay `str`-only in nanobind.

**Additional context**

Merge order: #9591 conflicts with #9611 in `FingerprintGeneratorWrapper.cpp`, `MorganWrapper.cpp`, `rdMolDraw2D.cpp`, `MaxMinPicker.cpp`, `testGenerators.py` and `testMolDraw2D.py`, where #9611 changes the bodies of functions whose signatures #9591 types, and with #9597 in `External/ChemDraw/nbWrap/rdChemDraw.cpp` and `testChemDraw.py`, which both change. Whichever of each pair lands second needs a merge there. #9612 merges cleanly with all three. #9619 changes `rdChemReactions.cpp` and `MaxMinPicker.cpp`, which #9611 also changes, so whichever lands second needs a merge in those two. A pull request that changes nanobind signatures and lands after #9613, such as #9597's ChemDraw readers, also needs its modules' stubs regenerated with the `nanobind_stubs` target, or `testTyping.py` fails.

Local test aborts: in local macOS builds, `rough_test.py`'s `testMolBundles1`, `FilterCatalog`'s `test0FilterCatalogEntry`, `SynthonSpaceSearch`'s `testBestHit`, `testEnumerations.py`, the serialization tests of `GeneralizedSubstruct`, `ScaffoldNetwork` and `TautomerQuery`, and destroying a Boost `MolDraw2DSVG` abort with `pointer being freed was not allocated` in `std::locale::~locale()`. The build used Apple's `clang++`, so RDKit links the system `/usr/lib/libc++.1.dylib`, while conda-forge's Boost links conda's own `libc++`; a locale created by one runtime is destroyed by the other, in four of the five inside Boost.Serialization's text archives. This comes from that environment rather than the RDKit code; building RDKit and Boost against one C++ runtime, for example with conda-forge's compilers, should avoid it, though that has not been tried. Separately, `SynthonSpaceSearch`'s `testShapePossibleHitsWrite` aborts and `testShapeInterimFile` hangs waiting for the restart file its child process should write, with or without these changes; neither has been traced.

RDKit's CI runs one pull request at a time, so earlier pull requests covering the same idea were folded into the above: #9593, #9594, #9596, #9598, #9599, #9600, #9602 and #9609 into #9591, #9603 into #9597, #9610 into #9611, and #9590, #9592 and #9595 into #9612.
